Before you begin

Work in pairs. One person runs the supplied code, the other reads the figure and writes the interpretation. Swap roles during the exercise. Predict before running each comparison. All required code is complete.

Use the prepared browser R environment. If access fails, open this HTML and the result sheet locally and answer the same questions. There is one core exercise today. Demonstrations and optional extensions are labelled. No installation, independent Stan programming or homework is required.

library(tidyverse)
library(posterior)
library(bayesplot)
library(patchwork)
library(here)
source(here("R/functions.R"))
source(here("R/course_data.R"))

theme_set(theme_bw(base_size=14))

Core exercise: survival at low and high conspecific density

Purpose Interpret the density relationship and its uncertainty on the probability scale.
Time 15 minutes: 10 minutes prediction, code and pair discussion, then 5 minutes explanation.
Computation Analyse the supplied day2_ndd fit. No new inference or compilation.
Data Seedlings and survivors in 60 simulated quadrats, with scaled conspecific density.

CNDD means conspecific negative density dependence. Today we ask whether seedling survival probability decreases with conspecific density. These simulated data illustrate the analysis. They are not observations from the research papers.

1. Predict the relationship (2 minutes)

ndd <- make_ndd_data()
ggplot(ndd, aes(cons, suv/n, size=n)) + geom_point(alpha=.65) +
  labs(x="Conspecific density (scaled)", y="Observed proportion surviving",
       size="Seedlings")

Which density would you expect to have higher survival probability? Write a prediction. Each point is a quadrat. Different quadrats can contain different numbers of seedlings.

2. Read the curve and intervals (5 minutes)

The model is the Day 1 binomial model with a density predictor:

s_i \sim \operatorname{Binomial}(n_i,p_i), \qquad \operatorname{logit}(p_i)=\alpha+\beta x_i.

The index i denotes a quadrat. x_i is scaled conspecific density. Both coefficients have independent Normal priors with mean 0 and SD 2.5. The model assumes a common probability within each quadrat and conditionally independent survival given that probability.

fit <- course_fit("day2_ndd")
draws <- fit$draws
fit$source
#> [1] "precomputed"
plot_cndd(draws, ndd)

Compare low density (x=-1, one SD below the mean) with high density (x=1, one SD above the mean). Keep the fitted data, model, prior and draws fixed. Only the prediction density changes.

probabilities <- cndd_probabilities(draws)
probability_summary <- probabilities |> group_by(density) |>
  summarise(median=median(p), lower=quantile(p,.05), upper=quantile(p,.95))
probability_summary
#> # A tibble: 2 × 4
#>   density median lower upper
#>     <dbl>  <dbl> <dbl> <dbl>
#> 1      -1  0.521 0.478 0.564
#> 2       1  0.170 0.135 0.209
plot_cndd_comparison(draws)

3. Explain the ecological result (3 minutes)

Complete this sentence with values and intervals from the table:

Predicted survival probability is ___ (90% interval ___ to ) at low density, compared with (___ to ___) at high density, under this model.

Does knowing a survival probability also determine the exact number of survivors in the next group of seedlings? Explain in one sentence.

TipSolution and instructor notes

Predicted survival is 0.52 (0.48 to 0.56) at low density, and 0.17 (0.14 to 0.21) at high density. These intervals describe uncertainty about each probability. Future survivor counts also vary randomly given the probability and the number of seedlings.

The negative density coefficient is on the logit scale. It is neither a probability difference nor a percent reduction. Transform every draw before summarising the probability. Hold the predictor values fixed when comparing answers.

This fitted association alone does not establish causation or show why rare species are rare. Species differences enter the conceptual research example on Day 3.

Instructor demonstrations

These are discussions during the lecture, not additional participant exercises.

Prior scale: the Normal regression illustration

The lecture uses the Normal-response example from main.qmd to ask whether a slope of 100 is sensible for the displayed units and ranges. It is a short illustration, not a second analysis exercise.

plot_normal_prior_scale()

For y_i\sim\mathcal{N}(a x_i+b,\sigma), a slope prior a\sim\mathcal{N}(0,2.5) uses SD 2.5 in the units of y per unit x. In CNDD the coefficients are on the logit scale. The same numerical SD does not imply the same ecological change. In both models, judge the implied predictions in the units of the question.

Computation and model code

course_diagnostics(fit)
#> # A tibble: 1 × 6
#>   max_rhat min_bulk_ess min_tail_ess divergent max_treedepth min_ebfmi
#>      <dbl>        <dbl>        <dbl>     <dbl>         <int>     <dbl>
#> 1     1.00        1698.        2123.         0             0      1.03
bayesplot::mcmc_trace(draws, pars=c("alpha","beta"))

Read R-hat, bulk/tail ESS, divergences, treedepth and E-BFMI together with the traces. Good computation diagnostics do not show whether the ecological model is adequate.

NoteCompleted Stan model 
data {
  int<lower=0> N;               // number of quadrats
  array[N] int<lower=0> n;      // seedlings per quadrat
  array[N] int<lower=0> suv;    // survivors per quadrat
  vector[N] cons;               // conspecific density (scaled)
}

parameters {
  real alpha;                   // intercept (logit scale)
  real beta;                    // slope (logit scale)
}

model {
  // likelihood: logit(p) = alpha + beta * cons
  suv ~ binomial_logit(n, alpha + beta * cons);
  // priors
  alpha ~ normal(0, 2.5);
  beta ~ normal(0, 2.5);
}

New seedling groups

Keep the same fit and compare new groups of 20 seedlings at the two densities. The code draws a probability from the posterior and then generates a binomial count.

predictions <- cndd_predictions(draws, n=20, seed=20261022)
plot_cndd_predictions(predictions)

The probability interval and the distribution of future survivor counts answer different questions. Counts can vary even if we know the probability precisely.

Model checking

Keep each observed quadrat’s density and seedling count fixed. Generate new survivor counts using posterior draws. Compare both the density pattern and the spread of survival proportions with the observations.

replicates <- cndd_replicates(draws, ndd, seed=20261023)
plot_cndd_check(replicates, ndd)
plot_cndd_spread_check(replicates, ndd)

Which parts look compatible? What would a systematic mismatch suggest? Because these data were generated from this model, we do not require a visible failure. A compatible plot alone does not establish ecological adequacy. Light, soils, shared enemies and species differences may matter in a real study.

TipSolution and instructor notes

The orange intervals in the first check are intervals for replicated proportions, including binomial variation at each observed n_i. They differ from the interval for p_i in the fitted-curve plot. Some observed points can lie outside 90% intervals. Do not count all such points as model failures. Look for systematic patterns.

The spread statistic checks one feature. A discrepancy could involve the density relationship, missing conditions or dependence among seedlings. It is not a uniquely identified diagnosis of a single ecological mechanism.

Optional extension: a probability difference

Use the same fit and paired posterior draws. Compute high-density minus low-density survival probability, then interpret the distribution. No refit is needed.

p_low <- plogis(draws$alpha-draws$beta)
p_high <- plogis(draws$alpha+draws$beta)
course_interval(p_high-p_low)
#> # A tibble: 1 × 4
#>     mean median  lower  upper
#>    <dbl>  <dbl>  <dbl>  <dbl>
#> 1 -0.351 -0.351 -0.413 -0.287
mean(p_high-p_low < 0)
#> [1] 1
TipSolution and instructor notes

A negative difference means lower predicted survival at high density for the specified comparison. The interval comes from paired differences, not from subtracting interval endpoints. Its units are probability points, not an odds ratio.

Reflection

What would you check before using this analysis on your own data? Tomorrow we ask how mother trees and species can differ while sharing information.
